o: After each obstacle insertion report the k-th smallest Manhattan distance from the origin, or −1 if fewer than k obstacles exist. We only ever need the k smallest distances, so a max-heap of size k suffices: push new distances while the heap is small; otherwise replace the top if the new distance is smaller. The k-th nearest is then always the heap top. Example 1 with k=2 evolves exactly as the samples show.
k: Maintain a max-heap capped at k distances.
New distance enters only if heap size < k or it beats the current k-th.
Answer is the heap root once size == k, else -1.

a.i: Simulate a max-heap with negated values in Python's min-heap. Each query does O(log k) work; total O(q log k). This is optimal for streaming k-th smallest maintenance.
s: For each (x, y): d = |x|+|y|; if len(heap) < k push −d; elif d < −heap[0] heapreplace.
a.t: O(q log k) — each insertion/replacement costs a heap operation

a.i: Keep all distances in a sorted array (binary search + insert). The k-th nearest is simply index k−1. Simpler to reason about but insertion is O(k) per query, giving O(q·k) — acceptable when q·k ≈ 2·10¹⁰ is too slow, so prefer the heap for the stated limits; included for completeness and small inputs.
s: Maintain a sorted array of distances.
Per query, binary search the insertion point and splice in d.
Append arr[k-1] if length ≥ k else -1.
a.t: O(q·k) — binary search is fast but array insertion shifts up to k elements

w: The bounded max-heap is the canonical streaming k-th-smallest technique — lead with it. Pitfalls: reporting −1 before the heap fills, and forgetting distances are Manhattan (|x|+|y|), not Euclidean. Follow-up: deletions of obstacles (need an indexed multiset / two-heaps balance), or k changing per query.
